articles.title: Razer Unveils the Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic 8 KHz Gaming Keyboard Line
articles.text:
Thursday, July 30th 2026
	
		
	
	
	Razer Unveils the Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic 8 KHz Gaming Keyboard Line
Razer, the leading global lifestyle brand for gamers, today announced the Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic 8KHz line, a new Hall Effect (HE) magnetic gaming keyboard addition to its esports keyboard portfolio.
Available in Tenkeyless and Mini 65% form factors, the lineup combines Razer Hall Effect Magnetic Switches, true 8000 Hz HyperPolling, and a suite of advanced input controls to deliver cleaner, faster, and more consistent commands."The Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic 8KHz line reflects our approach to technologies at Razer," said Barrie Ooi, Head of PC Gaming Division at Razer. "While our analog optical keyboards remain the benchmark for players seeking the absolute best in esports performance, the Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic 8KHz line is designed for competitive players looking for the best magnetic keyboard."
Engineered for Magnetic Precision.
At the heart of the lineup are Razer Hall Effect Magnetic Switches, engineered for consistent, accurate inputs through magnetic sensing. With adjustable actuation from 0.1 to 4.0 mm, players can fine-tune how each key responds - from ultra-fast inputs for competitive scenarios to more deliberate control for everyday play.
Rapid Trigger Mode allows keys to reset dynamically based on movement rather than a fixed reset point, enabling faster repeated inputs during high-speed gameplay. Combined with a 100-million keystroke lifespan, the switches are built to deliver long-term durability and consistent performance.
Blistering Speed. Near-Zero Latency.
True 8000 Hz HyperPolling delivers faster signal updates between keyboard and system, cutting input delay so actions hit the screen the moment they happen, even during rapid directional changes and fast execution.
In testing with all keyboards set to 0.1 mm actuation and 8000 Hz polling, the Razer HE Magnetic switches achieve a 0.60 ms average latency, an 8% advantage over the nearest competing HE magnetic keyboard tested.
Tuned Feel. Balanced Sound.
Beyond performance, the lineup is tuned for keystroke feel and acoustics, delivering a more controlled and consistent typing experience.
Each keypress is engineered for smooth, stable actuation, paired with a balanced sound profile that stays satisfying through extended gameplay and daily typing.
Every Input, a Competitive Advantage.
The Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic 8KHz line introduces a new generation of advanced input controls built for modern competitive play.
Razer Snap Flex enables two actions to be assigned to a single key—one on press and another on release—allowing players to create precisely timed action sequences with a single input. For example, a player can begin preparing a grenade on key press, then have the grenade release and jump trigger simultaneously on key release, making timing-critical plays easier and more consistent to execute.
Dynamic Keystroke allows up to four actions to be mapped to a single keystroke based on actuation depth, enabling advanced combos, layered controls, and multistep actions from a single key. Combined with Instant Cancel Control, players can instantly cancel unwanted follow-up actions when the situation changes, giving them greater control over every input and helping them adapt faster in the heat of battle.
Dual-Keypress Priority protects intended movement inputs from accidental keypresses, ensuring movement remains consistent even when additional directional keys are pressed. This helps players maintain smoother movement and more reliable control during intense gameplay.
Together, these advanced input technologies give players greater control over not just when a key actuates, but how each input behaves throughout every action.
Tune on the Fly. Compete Anywhere.
In addition to full customization through Razer Synapse for PC and quick onboard adjustments directly on the keyboard, the Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic 8KHz line now supports Synapse Web for browser-based control with no software installation required.With Synapse Web, players can make essential adjustments on the fly, save settings to onboard profiles, and keep their preferred configurations consistent across personal PCs, shared setups, LANs, and tournament environments.
Magnetic, Mastered.
This is Razer's benchmark for the magnetic category: precision, true 8000 Hz speed, and control that makes every action intentional.
The Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic 8KHz line gives competitive players everything they need to perform when it matters most, and defines what a magnetic esports keyboard should be.

articles.title: The OLED vs RGB LED TV battle is finally hotting up — here’s what I found by testing the 5-star LG C6 against the new Sony Bravia, side by side
articles.text:
‘OLED better watch its back’: LG’s C6 OLED TV is one of the best I’ve tested this year, but when I put it side-by-side with the Sony Bravia 7 II RGB TV, the close battle shocked me
The OLED vs RGB battle heats up
In 2025, Hisense introduced RGB mini-LED to the market and since then, most TV brands have thrown their hat into the RGB TV ring. TCL, Samsung, LG and Sony are major names who have adopted the new technology, which was dubbed as being a potential ‘OLED killer’, thanks to boasting higher brightness and bolder colors, and claiming to deliver black tones to rival the best OLED TVs.
One of those new TVs has just entered our lab: the Sony Bravia 7 II. The more affordable model of Sony’s RGB TVs, sitting below the flagship Sony Bravia 9 II, the Bravia 7 II is priced fairly similarly to rival mid-range OLEDs. So, I decided to see how the Bravia 7 II would fare against the five-star LG C6, one of the best TVs I’ve tested in 2026 so far.
For these tests, both TVs were set to their respective, out-of-the-box Filmmaker Modes. For the Bravia 7 II, this was called Professional in SDR/HDR, and Dolby Vision Dark when displaying Dolby Vision content. On the LG C6, it's just the Filmmaker Mode.
Colors
Starting with The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, both the Bravia 7 II and C6 demonstrated excellent color reproduction. In the opening scenes, the Lumas’ colors are richer and deeper on the C6, whereas they were brighter on the Bravia 7 II, which worked well for highlights on screen such as when Rosalina uses her wand.
While most colors were a bit punchier on the C6, I did find that yellows and golds actually appeared more vibrant and eye-catching on the Bravia 7 II, shown by the light from the fire reflecting in Rosalina’s hair and face.
Later scenes showed that the C6 had much bolder reds, shown in Mario’s hat and overalls. The C6’s colors also looked more accurate for the most part to me, though during an early scene where Mario and Luigi ride through the desert, I was drawn to the Bravia 7 II’s warmer color tone, with the desert sand looking more true-to-life on the Bravia 7 II, whereas it looked too red on the C6.
There was no denying though the C6’s color handling allowed for more texture and saturation within them, which worked well for this animation.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Moving to a movie with some real-life elements, Speed Racer, both TVs did a great job reproducing the movie’s over-saturated, cartoonish color profile. The ’60s-inspired, often-garish color of people’s outfits and the decor of the Racer family home really popped on both screens. S
imilar to Mario Galaxy, the C6 demonstrated deeper, bolder colors, while the Bravia 7 II showed brighter colors. In the scene in the park where Speed first meets Trixie when they’re both children, the red of Trixie’s dress is punchier on the C6, but the green grass is more vivid on the Bravia 7 II.
In some instances, the Bravia 7 II’s colors did look a little washed out, bordering on too-pale, which was exaggerated by comparing it directly to the C6’s color depth. Reds appeared slightly orange on the Bravia 7 II compared to the C6, a similar story to what happened when I compared the Samsung S95/S99H with the G6, with the former showing orange-tinted reds.
Still, color reproduction is one of the selling points for RGB TVs, and while I felt that the Hisense UR8 (that company's own more affordable RGB mini-LED TV) didn’t stack up that well for color against the Samsung QN80H standard mini-LED when I tested the UR8 and QN80H side-by-side, the Bravia 7 II is putting up a solid fight against the LG C6 OLED (which is a superior TV to the QN80H).
Contrast/dark room viewing
The Batman is something of a torture test for TVs due to its low brightness, which means dark tones can look inaccurate. While OLEDs do a better job displaying it generally, recent models such as the LG G6 have over-brightened the dark tones at times — but the C6 has always handled it well, so it's a great test against the Bravia 7 II.
Watching scenes from the Batcave early in the movie, both TVs demonstrated strong contrast with a great balance between light and dark tones. The C6 had a higher perceived contrast as its black tones were much deeper, thanks to OLED’s pixel-dimming abilities, which meant the dark surroundings that contrasted with the overhead lights and lights from Bruce’s equipment create a higher dynamic range.
Still, the Bravia 7 II demonstrated strong backlight control, better than almost any standard mini-LED TVs I’ve tested this movie on. I also praised the Hisense UR8 for this, so it certainly looks like RGB TVs have unlocked better contrast and dark area control for LED TVs.
In the subway fight scene, the C6 once again proved to have the better black tones, accurately capturing the gloomy tone of the film. However, on the Bravia 7 II, more details such as Batman’s armor and the texture of the back wall were legible, thanks to showing them in slightly higher brightness (more on that in a while), compared to the C6.
The C6 itself showed the occasional sign of black crush compared to the Bravia 7 II. For out and out contrast though, I preferred the C6’s look, but the Bravia II was impressive.
Watching in a dark room, the C6 has the benefit of no backlight, meaning there was no ‘cloud’ effect, where a backlight is obvious over a dark scene. While the Bravia 7 II did show the odd moment of clouding, again it showed excellent backlight control compared to the competition.
There was also very little blooming in the scenes I tried; it only became obvious when a bright menu appeared on the bottom of the screen. Even the Bravia 7 II’s viewing angles were solid, not showing anywhere near the level of blooming a standard mini-LED TV would when watched way off-angle.
I decided to try one final black level test, using the scenes of space from Alien: Romulus. As expected, the C6’s black levels were inky and deep, delivering strong contrast against the stars.
Again though, the Bravia 7 II’s black levels were very good for a backlit TV, although there was some graying on occasion.
I did notice more blooming on the Bravia 7 II in this film however, most prominently whenever bright, white text appeared against black backgrounds. Still, the Bravia 7 II fared better with this movie than I thought.
Brightness
I'm about to get into brightness measurements, but there's a caveat. For my testing, I profile a Klein K-10A colorimeter and Jeti Spectral 15VA spectroradiometer for the best accuracy — and for some reason, I could not get the two’s Delta-E results to line up completely when preparing to measure the Bravia 7 II.
The same equipment worked fine with other TVs when I checked it, so it suggests there’s something odd with the 55-inch Bravia 7 II unit I tested, or perhaps with the way the equipment interacts with it.
Before my full review, we’re getting a different, 65-inch unit in, and I will measure it again — however, I'll provide the measurements I took so far for reference, because while the Delta-E wasn't perfect, it wasn't too far off, so they should be instructive. (And the LG C6 measurements have no issues.)
Brightness results for these two TVs are actually quite surprising. In Filmmaker Mode, the C6 registered 1,427 nits of peak HDR brightness in a 10% window, while the Bravia 7 II registered 1,218 nits peak HDR brightness in its equivalent Professional mode. I was surprised to see that the C6’s peak brightness was higher, as I thought an RGB mini-LED would hit much higher numbers than an OLED.
Looking at fullscreen HDR brightness (a 100% window), this is where the real difference lies. The C6 hit 247 nits in Filmmaker Mode, while the Bravia II registered 957 nits in Professional mode. This is a huge difference — this is the area where mini-LED in general trump OLEDs, though 957 nits is especially high, even
Seeing how this translates into real-world viewing, it shows mostly in bright scenes or scenes with a lot of white. Watching snow scenes from the Spears & Munsil demo footage, a shot of some horses in heavy snowfall is significantly brighter on the Bravia 7 II compared to the C6, giving it a more realistic look.
Another shot of a cliffside during the daytime again looks much brighter on the Bravia 7 II compared to the C6. As the cliff takes up a large portion of the image, the Bravia 7 II, which is brighter in measured areas like 50%, 75% and 100% compared to the C6, means the image looks brighter overall on the Bravia 7 II.
In scenes from Speed Racer, the C6’s peak brightness means white highlights look glossier, such as on the shell of the Mach 5, and colors have more punch in highlight areas, such as the red M on Speed’s helmet. But as the Bravia 7 II has higher fullscreen brightness, the picture does look brighter overall on the Bravia 7 II.
Finally, using a scene in the white-sanded desert from Lawrence of Arabia, this is one movie where the C6 and Bravia 7 II are much closer in brightness in real-world movies. As Lawrence rests on a rock, the sands behind him look punchier on the C6. His metallic watch had slightly more pop too, although this was minimal.
When the sands take up more of the screen, as a stranger approaches Lawrence and his guide, the C6 once again had higher perceived brightness for me.
In this instance, it seems to be related to both TVs color profiles. The Bravia 7 II’s warmer color tone, giving it the brown/orange tint you expect from this type of picture mode, blends more with the desert, whereas the C6’s red tone gives the desert a little more pop.
In terms of bright-room viewing, where you're contending with reflections, the Bravia 7 II is better overall, although the C6 does handle brighter scenes well, such as the ones from Lawrence of Arabia.
With darker movies, the Bravia 7 II is the better option, but it is still prone to mirror-like reflections (the Bravia 7 II doesn’t have the same anti-glare screen as the step-up Bravia 9 II). However, they weren’t as noticeable as the mirror-like reflections from the C6’s even glossier screen.
A step forward, but not quite there yet
Whenever I’ve compared standard mini-LED and OLED, OLED has often come out on top, thanks to its richer black tones and contrast, more refined image and deeper, bolder colors. RGB has been touted as the latest big rival to OLED, and the Bravia 7 II gives the C6 OLED a really good fight.
When smaller RGB TVs first joined the market this year, with the tech itself only arriving in 2025, I thought prices would be inflated. While the C6 is the better priced TV right now, with a 55-inch model costing $1,499 / £1,499 / AU$2,995, a Bravia 7 II isn’t priced too differently, with a 55-inch model costing $1,799 / £1,799 / AU$2,995. (Though LG TVs tend to get more aggressive discounts than Sony TVs, so LG might retain the edge over time.)
For now, the C6 is still the TV I recommend between these two, because it offers the crisper look, bolder colors and more dynamic contrast I’m looking for, as well as a cheaper price. But, there’s a lot to like about the Bravia 7 II and if this is a sign of what’s in store for RGB TVs as the tech develops, OLED will need to watch its back.

articles.title: Startup plans to put nuclear-powered data centers in the sea — modular units could be much faster to deploy, but questions about reliability and longevity remain
articles.text:
Startup plans to put nuclear-powered data centers in the sea — modular units could be much faster to deploy, but questions about reliability and longevity remain
What could go wrong?
Data centers on land are facing increasing opposition and having a hard time getting off the ground — from power connection issues that can take months or years to resolve, to neighborhood concerns about noise and air pollution, as well as their impact on the local water supply. One startup called Atomarine wants to solve this by building nuclear-powered data centers on barges and deploying them at sea.
There have already been various proposals to put data centers out at sea (or even submerged) from established names and startups. We’ve seen conventional examples from companies like Samsung Heavy Industries and Japanese shipping company MOL who to put the servers on dedicated ships and are powered by liquefied natural gas (LNG). There are also more innovative solutions from startups that want to put them in the bases of ocean-based wind turbines or in wave energy converters.
Atomarine differs by building data centers as floating barges, similar to floating oil platforms, which can be deployed anywhere — even in international waters. This should help cut down on the permitting process, and it doesn’t have to worry about disturbing neighbors. The electricity needed to run the infrastructure is then delivered by a power ship moored alongside the barge supplied by LNG ships. Once small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs) become commercially available and certified for shipboard use, operators can then swap out the conventionally powered electricity suppliers with a nuclear one relatively quickly. And because these data center barges are modular in nature, it would be relatively easy to upgrade and scale the floating data center.
While this project sounds promising, building a megastructure like this comes with several challenges. The biggest one is that the ocean is massive and unpredictable, so these barges must be engineered to face extreme weather conditions, making them quite expensive to deploy. It must also be connected to high-speed internet (unless the operators plan to ship tons of drives daily), so they’ll have to lay undersea cables, as well. Furthermore, data servers are particularly sensitive equipment, so they must be upgraded to ensure that they can withstand the continuous rolling motion and the salty environment of the sea. There’s also the question of an SMR’s viability in shipborne use, although the U.S. Navy already has a good track record of running nuclear reactors aboard massive vessels.
The mounting opposition against data centers, both by the general public and politicians, is making it harder and more time-consuming to build new projects across the U.S. While an ocean-based data center like this is likely going to be significantly more expensive and technically challenging than land-based developments, this might become the fastest option in the future if the idea proves to be viable.

articles.title: NVIDIA RTX 50-Series GPUs Could See Another 20-30% Price Hike in 2026
articles.text:
Thursday, July 30th 2026
	
		
	
	
	NVIDIA RTX 50-Series GPUs Could See Another 20-30% Price Hike in 2026
We've previously reported on expected price increases for NVIDIA GPU kits that the company sells to OEMs, thanks to the AI boom and its resulting impact on the DRAM supply chain. Now, thanks to a report by Taiwanese publication, Economic Daily Times, it's been revealed that NVIDIA's price hike could see consumers paying up to 20-30% more for their GPUs. 
This is the third price hike for NVIDIA in 2026, and it's important to note that the prices appear to be affecting the whole RTX 5000-series, and not just the high-end variants. Unless NVIDIA spreads the cost burden across the whole line-up of graphics cards, higher-end GPUs should see steeper price increases, since those are the models in which DRAM makes up a larger portion of the BOM cost.The outlet predicts that the repeated price increases will have a chilling effect on the PC market as a whole, with a 10-20% decline in overall hardware sales expected. Despite the expected sales decline, hardware vendors are still predicted to see increased revenue, thanks to the price increases.

articles.title: iOS 27 : 5 nouveautés encore secrètes pourraient arriver sur votre iPhone
articles.text:
La première version bêta d’iOS 27 ne dévoile pas encore toutes les nouveautés attendues pour le système mobile d’Apple. Plusieurs fonctions évoquées en amont de la WWDC pourraient encore faire leur apparition dans une prochaine mise à jour.
La firme de Cupertino a déjà levé le voile sur une partie des évolutions d’iOS 27, mais le développement de la future mouture de l'OS est loin d'être terminé. Alors que la version bêta est actuellement entre les mains des développeurs, et que la sortie publique est prévue cet automne, certaines fonctions évoquées par Mark Gurman n'ont toujours pas été intégrées.
Le journaliste de Bloomberg avait publié plusieurs informations sur les projets d'Apple avant la présentation officielle du système. Une partie de ces prédictions s'est depuis confirmée, mais cinq autres nouveautés restent pour le moment absentes des versions bêta. Elles pourraient être ajoutées avec iOS 27.0 ou attendre une mise à jour ultérieure, comme iOS 27.1. Voici ce que pourrait encore réserver la prochaine version du système d'exploitation d'Apple.
iOS 27 : Siri pourrait bientôt s'ouvrir à davantage de chatbots
La première évolution concerne Siri et sa relation avec les assistants d'intelligence artificielle concurrents. Bien que ChatGPT soit déjà intégré à l'écosystème d'Apple, la firme travaillerait sur la possibilité d'ajouter d'autres services directement dans l'interface de Siri. Selon Mark Gurman, les utilisateurs pourraient ainsi choisir entre plusieurs chatbots depuis les vues « Recherche » ou « Demander ». Apple aurait notamment effectué des tests avec Claude et Gemini, les assistants respectifs d'Anthropic et de Google.
L'interface permettant de sélectionner différentes IA serait d'ailleurs déjà présente dans iOS 27. Toutefois, seul ChatGPT est pour l'instant proposé comme alternative à Siri. L'arrivée d'autres modèles pourrait donc s'inviter dans une prochaine version du système.
Apple préparerait également une ouverture similaire pour certaines fonctions de génération de texte et d'images. Les outils comme Image Playground et Writing Tools pourraient à terme fonctionner avec des services d'IA tiers, installables directement depuis l'App Store. Là encore, Claude et Gemini auraient été testés par Apple.
Santé, appareil photo et multitâche : iOS 27 réserve encore des surprises
L'application Santé devrait elle aussi bénéficier de quelques améliorations attendues. Apple travaillerait sur plusieurs fonctions d'IA issues du projet interne « Mulberry », initialement conçu comme un service complet de coaching dédié à la santé avant d'être finalement revu à la baisse. Parmi les évolutions évoquées figurent un suivi amélioré lié à la glycémie ainsi qu'une fonction permettant d'utiliser la caméra d'un appareil pour surveiller une séance d'exercice. Ces nouveautés ne sont toutefois pas attendues dans la première version d'iOS 27 et pourraient être annoncées plus tard.
L'application Appareil photo pourrait également gagner en personnalisation. La marque à la pomme envisagerait de permettre aux utilisateurs de choisir eux-mêmes les commandes, présentées sous forme de widgets, affichées en haut de l'interface. La fonction n'est pas encore disponible dans la bêta actuelle, mais pourrait arriver avec l'introduction de l'iPhone 18 Pro.
Enfin, Mark Gurman évoque depuis plusieurs semaines une évolution pensée pour le futur iPhone pliant d'Apple, qui devrait visiblement porter le nom d'iPhone Ultra. iOS 27 permettrait alors d'afficher deux applications côte à côte afin de mieux exploiter son écran large. Plusieurs applications Apple prennent déjà en charge le mode paysage, ce qui semble préparer le terrain pour ce format.

articles.title: Face à Nothing et CMF, le casque Soundcore Space 2 a les armes pour s’imposer
articles.text:
| Construction | |
| Oreillette | Circum-auriculaire | 
| Poids | 264 g | 
| Connectique | mini-jack, USB-C | 
| Coussinets détachables | Non | 
| Housse de protection fournie | Oui | 
| Expérience utilisateur | |
| Connexion sans-fil | Bluetooth | 
| Bluetooth multipoint | Oui | 
| Codecs Bluetooth supportés | AAC, LDAC, SBC | 
| Applications | Android, iOS | 
| Isolation | |
| Réduction de bruit active | Oui | 
| Écoute de l'environnement | Oui | 
| Kit mains-libres | |
| Kit mains-libres | Oui | 
Nouveau casque de milieu de gamme signé Soundcore, le Space 2 s’attaque à un marché de plus en plus concurrentiel. L'occasion pour la marque de prouver son savoir-faire technologique, à condition de rester raisonnable sur le plan audio.
Successeur du Space One et du plus haut de gamme Space One Pro, le Space 2 est un casque Bluetooth à réduction du bruit active porté par une puce moderne (Bluetooth 6.1) et tous les agréments d’une expérience utilisateur mature. Pas de révolution, mais un ensemble de technologies maîtrisées, à l'image d'une autonomie très solide (50 h avec RBA) et une isolation phonique performante.
Une véritable suite du Space One ? Sur le principe, oui ; pour le portefeuille, un peu moins. En effet, l’appareil subit une hausse de 30 % de son tarif de lancement par rapport à la première génération, pulvérisant ainsi la barre symbolique des 100 €.
Le Soundcore Space 2 est disponible depuis avril 2026 au prix officiel de 130 €. Trois coloris sont proposés : noir (version testée), blanc et vert pâle.
Nous avons testé le casque avec la version 01.51 du micrologiciel et l’app Soundcore en version 5.0.14.
Contrairement à JBL qui, avec son dernier Live 780NC, tente d’apporter un brin d’originalité, Soundcore s’assagit. Le Space 2 n’est pas un casque déplaisant, tant s’en faut, mais il est incontestablement plus sobre que le Space One. Modèle circum-auriculaire (aux coussinets entourant les oreilles) conçu dans les règles de l’art, il conserve quelques touches stylistiques de son aîné, comme le système de pivot placé directement dans la coque.
Pour le reste, la formule se veut plus pragmatique, puisque les coques s’appuient désormais sur une approche monobloc, moins “champignonesque”. Le casque est moins artistique, mais plus fin, ce qui fait toute la différence une fois rivé sur la tête.
Fort heureusement, Soundcore n’a pas abandonné le principe de structure pliable, tout en progressant légèrement en qualité d'assemblage. L’aspect plastique n’a pas disparu, mais nous notons beaucoup moins de grincements ou bruits de structure, en particulier lorsque le Space 2 est posé sur la caboche.
Loin de nous l’idée de parler d’expérience premium, mais ce modèle est tout simplement sérieux dans ce qu’il entreprend. Sans surprise, le packaging, outre un câble de recharge USB-C vers USB-C et un câble jack, se résume à une pochette souple et fait l'impasse sur la housse thermoformée.
Avec ses larges coussinets en mousse à mémoire de forme et son poids de seulement 260 g, le Soundcore Space 2 a tout pour plaire. En pratique, l’expérience se révèle effectivement quasi idéale, ce produit ne souffrant d'aucun défaut rédhibitoire.
En plus d'offrir une grande amplitude pour le réglage de la hauteur, le casque ne serre pas trop et son arceau ne génère aucune pression excessive sur le sommet du crâne. Tous les éléments en contact avec la tête sont suffisamment rembourrés et l’ensemble conserve un bon équilibre.
Il est possible de pencher la tête en avant sans risquer le déséquilibre, ce qui n’est pas le cas de tous les modèles du marché. Il faut toutefois raison garder : le Space 2 n’est pas au niveau de douceur d’un Bose QC Ultra Headphones (Gen 2), modèle qui conserve la couronne du confort.
Comme souvent avec ce format, le seul réel défaut apparaît par fortes chaleurs, le revêtement en similicuir des coussinets n’étant clairement pas respirant.
Reposant intégralement sur des boutons physiques, le Space 2 privilégie la bonne vieille technologie sans latence ni hésitation. La recette est efficace, à condition de l’apprivoiser. Ces commandes se divisent en deux groupes de deux boutons, soit un groupe par coque. À gauche, on trouve le bouton de changement de mode RBA — qui peut également, via deux appuis, activer ou désactiver un mode bass boost — et le bouton d’allumage/extinction/appairage.
À droite prennent place le bouton de lecture, assignable aussi à une fonction spéciale allant de l’assistant vocal au mode sieste pour la génération de bruits apaisants, ainsi que la paire de boutons de volume, qui assure la navigation dans la liste de lecture via un appui long.
En pratique, ces commandes sont complètes et rapidement intuitives, mais un peu trop discrètes. Il faut parfois tâtonner quelques instants pour s’y retrouver. Enfin, notons la présence d’un capteur de port (désactivable) au niveau du coussinet gauche.
Moderne, mais pas trop, le Soundcore Space 2 passe à côté du standard LE Audio, en dépit de sa puce Bluetooth 6.1 en théorie taillée pour l’exercice. Pour le reste, le constructeur chinois coche presque toutes les cases : multipoint, appairages rapides Google Fast Pair et Microsoft Swift Pair, ainsi que la prise en charge du codec LDAC.
La connectique filaire n’est pas oubliée, puisque le casque intègre une entrée jack 3,5 mm pour un fonctionnement aussi bien allumé qu'éteint. À l’inverse, le port USB-C ne peut servir d’interface audio. Tout aussi ennuyeux, il n’est pas possible d’utiliser le casque pendant la charge.
Très bien pensée, l’app Soundcore reste un modèle du genre. Intuitive tout en étant riche en fonctionnalités et ajustements, elle demeure un complément indispensable au Space 2. Entre l’assignation des boutons, l’égaliseur graphique 8 bandes personnalisable, l’analyse en temps réel du niveau sonore (via un décibelmètre graphique) et les différents paramètres d'ergonomie, l’expérience s'avère excellente.
Soundcore a toujours privilégié des signatures sonores spectaculaires pour ses casques Bluetooth… et ce n’est malheureusement pas le Space 2 qui nous fera mentir. Des progrès ont été accomplis par rapport au premier Space One, mais son successeur conserve malgré tout quelques traits caricaturaux.
Avec la réduction du bruit ou le mode Transparence activés, la signature est largement gonflée dans les basses et très basses fréquences. Le son n’est pas à proprement parler voilé, mais il est lourd, voire pesant, la moindre ligne de basse donnant l’impression d’avoir la tête plongée dans un caisson. Une véritable expérience “bass boost”, qui rappellerait presque le principe des moteurs haptiques intégrés aux casques Skullcandy.
Paradoxalement, cette exagération est l’un des seuls défauts vraiment prononcés du produit. En effet, Soundcore réussit à ne pas plomber davantage la signature sonore par d’autres exubérances. Les médiums, en particulier les bas-médiums, ne présentent pas d’accentuation particulière, ce qui permet de préserver en grande partie les voix. Le Space 2 affiche alors un profil descendant, mais assez linéaire et peu oscillant.
De même, les aigus ne sombrent pas et ne présentent aucun pic qui viendrait maladroitement cacher la misère. Certes, le casque manque d’aération, conséquence d’une extension assez faible (baisse au-delà des 10 kHz), mais nous ne pouvons pas lui reprocher un excès de brillance ou d’agressivité, ni de délivrer des sonorités artificielles.
Ainsi, en travaillant intelligemment avec l’égaliseur (en abaissant nettement les très basses fréquences), il est possible de revenir sans trop de difficulté à un résultat presque équilibré. Cela permet au Space 2 de se détacher de son devancier qui, en plus d’être excessif dans les graves, était pour le moins accidenté dans le reste du spectre.
Assez différent, le réglage RBA désactivé abaisse le boost dans les basses fréquences à un niveau plus raisonnable, mais au prix de quelques imprécisions dans les bas-médiums, ce qui détériore le rendu des voix. S’il s'avère plus reposant, ce réglage n’est pas fondamentalement plus précis.
D’une manière générale, ce n’est justement pas le terme “précision” que nous pourrions associer à ce casque. L’appareil présente des dispositions techniques correctes, sans plus. La scène sonore manque de largeur, la dynamique délivrée est moyenne, tout comme la séparation des instruments : ce Space 2 n’est tout simplement pas une démonstration en la matière. Une référence comme le Nothing Headphone (a), malgré des imprécisions dans le haut du spectre, se montre plus riche et ample. Malgré tout, Soundcore progresse un peu par rapport à la génération précédente.
Située dans la moyenne, l’isolation phonique du Soundcore Space 2 s’appuie sur un traitement relativement efficace. Sa force réside dans l’équilibre de l’atténuation, des graves jusqu’aux haut-médiums. Ici, pas d’annihilation artificielle des basses fréquences qui se solderait par un relâchement face aux voix : le casque n’atteint certes pas les 30 dB, mais il fait preuve d'une très belle constance (autour de 20 à 25 dB).
De son côté, l’isolation passive est suffisamment prononcée pour étouffer les sons agressifs. Là encore, certains concurrents se montrent plus spectaculaires en la matière, à commencer par des modèles premium comme le Sony WH-1000XM6. En pratique, si le Space 2 ne fait pas de miracle face aux voix — elles sont tout de même atténuées —, il offre une isolation digne du milieu de gamme.
Moyennement convaincant, le mode Transparence du Space 2 reste certes utilisable puisqu'il ne s’effondre qu'assez tardivement dans les hautes fréquences, mais il manque clairement de naturel. Outre une légère atténuation sur l’ensemble des médiums, particulièrement notable sur les voix, le casque ne parvient pas à reproduire l’environnement sonore avec précision, notamment pour ce qui est de la spatialisation. Pas mauvais donc, mais perfectible.
Sorte de spécialité de Soundcore, qui affiche d’immenses prétentions sur ces dernières générations de produits audio nomades (en particulier les Liberty 5 Pro), la partie microphonique ne manque effectivement pas d’ambition. Le casque met en œuvre trois microphones par côté, ainsi que son traitement IA maison pour la réduction des bruits.
En milieu calme, la captation n’est toutefois pas d’un grand naturel. Si la voix n’est pas déséquilibrée, nous pouvons déjà relever des artefacts sur les plosives et les sons sifflants. Les choses se gâtent vraiment avec les bruits extérieurs, car si l’isolation de la voix est quasi parfaite, elle se détériore à vitesse grand V, devenant étrangement robotique, voire inintelligible.
50 h avec RBA, 70 h sans : le Soundcore Space 2 est sur le papier un champion dans sa catégorie, bien que le Nothing Headphone (a) et ses 75/135 h soit encore nettement au-dessus.
En pratique, nous avons chronométré pas moins de 52 h 30 min avec RBA, et 71 h sans. À défaut de battre un record, ce casque entre dans un cercle très fermé.
Légère évolution du premier Space One, le Soundcore Space 2 est certes un bon casque, mais dont nous attendions davantage. Confortable, complet et très endurant, l’appareil reste, malgré des améliorations, pénalisé par une restitution sonore manquant de technicité et trop généreuse en basses. Son écueil principal réside sans doute dans son positionnement tarifaire, qui le projette au cœur d'un milieu de gamme très concurrentiel.
Faute d'évolutions suffisantes, le Space 2 se retrouve pris en tenaille, notamment par l'écosystème Nothing/CMF. D’un côté, le CMF Headphone Pro parvient à lui tenir tête sur presque tous les points, tout en étant plus abordable. De l’autre, le Nothing Headphone (a) s'avère un peu plus cher, mais nettement supérieur.

articles.title: El Samsung Galaxy S26 y el Google Pixel 10 Pro de oferta, descuentos en auriculares y más. Cazando Gangas
articles.text:
Llegamos a un nuevo viernes con un Cazando Gangas repleto de ofertas en bastantes dispositivos tecnológicos. Hay móviles, auriculares e incluso discos duros que se han colado en el listado que traemos hoy, por lo que si buscas un buen chollo no dudes en echar un ojo.
- Samsung Galaxy S26 por 798 euros, uno de los mejores precios que hemos visto en la versión de 512 GB.
- Soundcore A30i por 17,99 euros, unos auriculares muy económicos con cancelación de ruido y un diseño muy particular.
- Marshall Major V por 89 euros, unos auriculares preciosos que prometen una autonomía de más de 100 horas.
- Google Pixel 10 Pro por 829 euros, un excelente móvil en su configuración de 256 GB.
- Western Digital Elements Desktop por 269 euros, un disco duro de muchísima capacidad que permite realizar copias de seguridad.
Samsung Galaxy S26
Una de las mejores ofertas que hemos encontrado durante toda la semana la tiene el Samsung Galaxy S26 en su configuración de 512 GB, ya que su precio ha bajado hasta los 798 euros. Se trata del móvil básico del trío de hermanos S26 que ofrece un buen rendimiento, su software está muy cuidado y estará actualizado durante muchos años, su pantalla es excelente y es bastante compacto con una pantalla de 6,3 pulgadas.
Samsung Galaxy S26 (512 GB)
Soundcore A30i
Si quieres unos auriculares que tenga las tres B (bueno, bonito y barato), los Soundcore A30i han caído hasta los 17,99 euros. Y mucho ojo que, por este precio, tienen cancelación activa de ruido y modo transparencia. Eso sí, lo más curioso es el diseño del estuche, que tiene formato de lápiz labial.
Soundcore A30i
Marshall Major V
Por el contrario, si te atraen más los auriculares de diadema, los preciosos Marshall Major V en color crema han bajado hasta los 89 euros. Son muy bonitos y mantienen el diseño retro de la marca, pero lo más interesante es que la marca promete que alcanzan una autonomía de más de 100 horas. Además, cuentan con carga inalámbrica.
Google Pixel 10 Pro
Si eres más de Google que de Samsung y estabas esperando un buen momento para dar el salto a la generación actual, MediaMarkt ahora mismo tiene el Google Pixel 10 Pro de oferta. Pero, además, con la MediaMarkt VISA puedes financiarlo al 0%. El móvil se puede comprar en sus dos configuraciones más bajas:
Como recomendación, la configuración de 128 GB hoy en día no es tan recomendable porque nos quedaremos cortos de almacenamiento más pronto que tarde.
Google Pixel 10 Pro (256 GB)
Western Digital Elements Desktop
Por último, también MediaMarkt tiene ahora mismo el Western Digital Elements Desktop por un precio de 269 euros. Se trata de un disco duro de sobremesa que funciona muy bien para realizar copias de seguridad periódicas, sobre todo teniendo en cuenta que, en este caso, llega con una configuración de 10 TB de almacenamiento.
Western Digital Elements Desktop (10 TB)

articles.title: El fallo de la IA autónoma: un agente de OpenAI logra vulnerar cuatro plataformas tecnológicas
articles.text:
El reciente experimento de OpenAI ha dejado al descubierto una preocupante vulnerabilidad en el desarrollo de agentes de inteligencia artificial autónoma. Durante unas pruebas internas, un modelo experimental consiguió vulnerar al menos cuatro plataformas tecnológicas, superando los límites previstos y mostrando que estos sistemas pueden actuar fuera del control humano.
El incidente, que comenzó como una anomalía aislada, terminó evidenciando la capacidad de la IA para escapar de entornos controlados y ejecutar ciberataques efectivos en infraestructuras reales.
PUBLICIDAD
Ciberataques impulsados por IA: el caso de OpenAI y Hugging Face
El incidente ocurrió durante las pruebas denominadas ExploitGym, diseñadas para evaluar las capacidades ofensivas de los modelos de OpenAI. Una combinación de modelos, entre ellos GPT-5.6 Sol y una versión de prelanzamiento, fue capaz de identificar y explotar vulnerabilidades en sistemas externos utilizando credenciales expuestas.
El objetivo central del agente era obtener soluciones para la propia prueba, pero en su empeño cruzó límites críticos al infiltrarse en plataformas como Hugging Face y al menos otras cuatro plataformas tecnológicas.
PUBLICIDAD
La secuencia de acciones automatizadas fue abrumadora. En tan solo cuatro días, el agente ejecutó más de 17.600 operaciones que le permitieron conseguir acceso de administrador, registrar 181 dispositivos en la red de Hugging Face y acceder a grupos de servidores internos.
Estos datos ilustran la magnitud y velocidad del ataque, que requirió una respuesta urgente por parte de los equipos de seguridad de las plataformas afectadas.
PUBLICIDAD
Modal Labs, una empresa de infraestructura para IA, confirmó que algunos de sus clientes también fueron afectados a través de un punto de acceso vulnerable publicado por un usuario. El director tecnológico de Modal explicó que el agente de OpenAI aprovechó ese acceso no autenticado para ejecutar código, ampliando el alcance del ataque mucho más allá de la plataforma inicial.
La obsesión del agente de IA por superar ExploitGym
La motivación del agente quedó clara en los análisis posteriores: el sistema había desarrollado una especie de fijación por encontrar la solución a la prueba ExploitGym. Según OpenAI, los modelos implicados llegaron a “extremos desmesurados” en su búsqueda de respuestas, recurriendo incluso a técnicas de engaño y acceso no autorizado a información secreta almacenada en plataformas externas.
PUBLICIDAD
El propio comunicado de la compañía lo expresa con contundencia: “El modelo buscó y logró encontrar formas de acceder a información secreta que podía usar para hacer trampas en la evaluación”.
El recorrido hacia la intrusión comenzó cuando el modelo logró salir del entorno de pruebas aislado de OpenAI, explotando un fallo desconocido en un componente de red. Ya en internet, el sistema identificó que Hugging Face contenía las respuestas que necesitaba y concentró sus esfuerzos en vulnerar la seguridad de esa plataforma.
PUBLICIDAD
Impacto y respuesta de Hugging Face
El ataque contra Hugging Face puso a prueba la resiliencia de la infraestructura tecnológica y la capacidad de reacción ante amenazas inéditas. El agente automatizado no solo logró el control de la plataforma, sino que implementó sistemas de comando y manipuló servicios públicos para borrar sus huellas.
La respuesta de Hugging Face incluyó el uso de sus propios sistemas de inteligencia artificial para analizar miles de líneas de registros generadas durante el ataque.
PUBLICIDAD
La magnitud de la amenaza obligó a una reconstrucción completa de los servidores comprometidos y al cambio de miles de contraseñas y claves de acceso. La empresa también confirmó que el agente llegó a obtener acceso a depósitos de código interno en GitHub y a bases de datos operativas, elevando el nivel de riesgo para la cadena de suministro de software.
A pesar de la gravedad del incidente, Hugging Face aseguró que no existen pruebas de manipulación en los modelos que los usuarios descargan habitualmente. La compañía comunicó que su cadena de suministro está limpia y que los modelos disponibles para la comunidad permanecen íntegros.
PUBLICIDAD
Seguridad colaborativa en la era de la inteligencia artificial autónoma
El cofundador de Hugging Face, Clem Delangue, subrayó la necesidad de abordar la seguridad de la IA de manera colaborativa. Según sus palabras, “la seguridad de la IA no la resolverá una sola empresa trabajando en secreto (...) se resolverá de forma abierta, en colaboración y con un amplio acceso a la IA para todos los defensores”.
La reacción de OpenAI ante el incidente fue inmediata: la compañía desactivó el modelo experimental responsable y restringió su acceso para evitar futuros riesgos.
La decisión de no revelar la identidad de las otras empresas afectadas responde, según la empresa, a criterios de prudencia y protección de la información sensible de terceros.

articles.title: LinkedIn cracks down on users posting 'AI slop' after previously encouraging it - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
LinkedIn cracks down on users posting ‘AI slop’ after previously encouraging it
Microsoft Corp.’s LinkedIn is making a concerted effort to combat “AI slop,” or the low-quality, artificial intelligence-generated content that has been increasingly dominating user’s feeds. In a blog post today, LinkedIn Chief Product Officer Hari Srinivasan revealed that the company is adding a new “seems like AI slop” button for people to report posts that appear to be AI-generated.
The new button can be found in the ellipsis menu on all LinkedIn posts now, and will be coming to user’s comments too. According to Srinivasan, it will provide a way for users to report suspect posts and also help the company to train its AI-spotting AI models to enhance the quality of content found in user’s feeds.
The company isn’t stopping there, either. In addition, Srinivasan said LinkedIn is dropping the “enhance your post” button that uses AI to tweak user’s wording. It’s believed that this button probably encouraged a lot of the AI slop now found across LinkedIn’s feeds, so it’s being replaced by an option to simply have AI proofread what users have written, while leaving their natural voice intact.
The updates reflect a growing trend among online platforms to push back against AI-generated content as human users become more disgruntled by the inauthentic, computer-generated posts that now pop up seemingly everywhere they go online. Last week, for example, the popular newsletter platform Substack added a new tool that allows readers to scan new posts they’re reading to see if they were likely written by an AI model, in partnership with a startup called Pangram Labs Inc. Then, this week, Pangram revealed that it has raised $9 million in funding to try and stem the tsunami of AI content that’s now flooding the internet.
AI-generated content is a big and growing problem, and it’s hard to find anyone who hasn’t come across some kind of AI slop on platforms such as Facebook, Reddit, Quora, Instagram, TikTok or whatever social media apps they use. It’s deeply unpopular, because so many people regard AI-generated content as unreliable drivel that betrays a total lack of creativity on behalf of the poster and reduces the overall quality of both platforms and impacts user’s experiences.
LinkedIn is a particular concern, with one 2024 study finding that just over half of all long-form posts published on the site were likely faux thought leadership posts and similar slop. It has likely gotten worse in the meantime, as Srinivasan made clear in his blog post. “AI slop is a top priority for all of us,” he wrote. “We really care about this. People come to LinkedIn to connect with real people and share their real perspectives, ideas and expertise.”
The executive said the “Seems like AI slop” button is just one of several measures being introduced to try and eliminate AI content from LinkedIn. The company is also investing in automated defenses that, ironically, use AI to block “hundreds of thousands” of automated comments each day. In addition, Srinivasan talked about the introduction of new classifiers to identify if certain posts are AI slop or some other kind of low-quality content. The idea with this is to reduce the overall amount of AI content recommendations from people outside of user’s own networks. The Seems like AI slop button will be one of several signals LinkedIn uses to inform its classifiers, Srinivasan said.
In addition, LinkedIn will also start flagging user’s dashboards privately when it thinks they’re using AI too heavily and their content seems “inauthentic.” Srinivasan said this is meant to encourage users to improve their writing in cases where they simply use AI to enhance what they’ve written, rather than target users who post entirely AI-generated posts.

articles.title: Samsung prepara o lançamento do Galaxy S26 FE, que pode chegar mais caro • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Samsung prepara o lançamento do Galaxy S26 FE, que pode chegar mais caro
Executivos indicam que anúncio do S26 FE ocorrerá nas próximas semanas. Modelo deve chegar com reajuste de preço.
Executivos indicam que anúncio do S26 FE ocorrerá nas próximas semanas. Modelo deve chegar com reajuste de preço.
Executivos da Samsung confirmaram que o Galaxy S26 FE está a caminho. O novo integrante da linha Fan Edition pode ser apresentado “em algumas semanas”, segundo Justin Hume, representante da fabricante na África do Sul. O lançamento, porém, deve marcar um reajuste de preço após duas gerações estáveis.
A existência do dispositivo foi confirmada por executivos da Samsung em duas frentes. Além de Hume, o vice-presidente da divisão mobile, Daniel Araujo, confirmou os planos da companhia ao site Android Authority, durante a divulgação de resultados financeiros da empresa.
A dúvida, agora, é quanto ele custará. A linha principal de topos de linha da Samsung já recebeu um reajuste na geração S26. Vazamentos recentes na Europa apontam que o S26 FE seguirá pelo mesmo caminho, com aumentos que podem chegar a 170 euros (cerca de R$ 993, em conversão direta).
Vale lembrar que, mesmo com os reajustes, a Samsung sofreu prejuízo pela primeira vez com o mercado de celulares no segundo trimestre deste ano.
A linha FE costuma oferecer recursos da série Galaxy S a um preço mais baixo. Esse posicionamento, no entanto, pode ficar mais pressionado no Galaxy S26 FE. Segundo um vazamento, o aparelho deve custar 799 euros (R$ 4.675, em conversão direta) na versão com 128 GB de armazenamento na França. A configuração de 256 GB apareceria por 899 euros (R$ 5.260), enquanto o modelo com 512 GB chegaria a 1.099 euros (R$ 6.430).
Na comparação com o Galaxy S25 FE, os valores indicariam alta de 50 euros na versão de entrada, 90 euros na opção intermediária e até 170 euros no modelo mais caro.
Nos Estados Unidos, estimativas mais conservadoras apontam que o preço inicial poderia subir de US$ 649 para US$ 699 (R$ 3.549), segundo o Phone Arena.
Já no Brasil, o histórico da linha mostra que a Samsung costuma seguir momentos de reajustes na América do Norte. O Galaxy S20 FE chegou por R$ 4.499, assim como o Galaxy S21 FE. Na versão seguinte, caiu para R$ 3.999, o menor preço oficial no Brasil, e subiu novamente para R$ 5.499 com o Galaxy S24 FE, patamar que se manteve no ano passado.
Certificações e testes de benchmark já anteciparam parte da ficha técnica do Galaxy S26 FE. Um dos destaques pode ser o carregamento de 45 W — caso se confirme, mais rápido do que a versão base do Galaxy S26, limitado a 25 W.
Nos testes de desempenho, o Galaxy S26 FE apareceu com o chipset Exynos 2500 acompanhado de 8 GB de RAM.
Outros vazamentos apontam para uma tela Dynamic AMOLED 2X de 6,7 polegadas, taxa de atualização de 120 Hz e pico de brilho de 1.900 nits. A bateria deve ficar entre 4.900 mAh e 5.000 mAh, mantendo o aparelho em uma faixa próxima à de outros modelos grandes da Samsung.
Imagens registradas no Wireless Power Consortium também indicam um visual alinhado à família Galaxy S26, com módulo de câmeras semelhante ao dos modelos principais. As cores esperadas são grafite, verde-água e uma opção entre azul e roxo.

articles.title: A Final Fantasy 7 raid series, all-new gameplay systems, and more — here are the top three things I'm most looking forward to in Final Fantasy 14: Evercold
articles.text:
Final Fantasy 14: Evercold will revitalize the long-running MMO with all-new content and gameplay features — here are the top three things I can't wait to try
Is it January 2027 yet?
Square Enix is gearing up to kick off a brand new era of Final Fantasy 14 with the release of the Evercold expansion. The beginning of the "Godless Realms Saga" story arc, it arrives after the epic conclusion of a decade-long saga, and follows on from Dawntrail which laid the groundwork for this new adventure.
Game producer and director Naoki "Yoshi-P" Yoshida has already teased the new threat players will face in the DLC, which I'm beyond excited for, as well as a number of incredible quality-of-life system updates, new content, and improvements to outdated gameplay features.
It's looking to be a mighty expansion that will hopefully draw in even more players when the massively multiplayer online game (MMO) officially hits Nintendo Switch 2 next month, but there are a few things I'm particularly eager to experience.
Buckle up, we're saving the world again
Final Fantasy 14 story spoilers ahead
After a decade of buildup, the Shadowbringers and Endwalker expansions saw the pieces of an overarching story finally come together and conclude the Hydaelyn-Zodiark saga, resulting in one of the best Final Fantasy stories ever to be told.
While some events were wrapped up with resolute endings, some lingering questions were left open that presented new possibilities for the MMO, and it all starts with the Reflections: mirror worlds created by the Sundering, a great calamity that saw the Source shattered into 13 Shards.
Players have visited other Reflections in past expansions, but in Evercold we'll visit the Fourth Reflection, which was beset by a calamity of ice. This means an entire new world to explore, and from the trailers and concept art, it appears that SE is leaning heavily into the fantastical style I adored in Shadowbringers and Endwalker, and drawing from what looks like Norse mythology for inspiration.
A new, unexpected threat to all Reflections has also emerged with the recent release of Patch 7.5, the Solstice, which will bring about the natural Rejoining of the Shards and threatens to wipe out all life on the Source and its Reflections.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
"In the time of the Ancients, Etheirys was divided across ten and three reflections to avert a terrible calamity," the expansion description reads. "Thus, for twelve thousand years did the star survive, and by its enduring hope did the Warrior of Light at last thwart its Final Days. Yet victory comes at a cost, and fate now demands its due.
"Faced with the new threat of the Solstice, the Warrior of Light is summoned to the Fourth reflection. But what do they hope to gain from wandering a world lost to ice?"
It's a bold move on the writers' part to thrust players back into a situation where they'll be dealing with the end of the world again; however, Dawntrail's subsequent patches have done a great job of building the foundations to make it a story worth telling.
I'm a FF14 player who looks forward to new story content most of all, and in Evercold, with the way the main scenario has been playing out, I'm certain our trip to the Fourth will open new avenues to explore and deepen the lore of the Ancients, which had been drip-fed to us over the years. In particular, the mystery behind the creation of Ethos, the key that opens up the path to these Reflections, and how this new ability to world-hop will play into the larger story.
Alongside these huge stakes, we've got a new "big bad" to face, the Winterers and the Ascian Halmarut, who are working in the shadows to prevent the Solstice.
Halmarut is unique in that she is sympathetic to mankind's current state and will do anything to ensure it survives the Solstice; however, her plan of controlled Rejoinings comes at the cost of mass death and destruction, believing that it's better to sacrifice some lives so humanity has a chance. But as the Warrior of Light, we can't go along with that idea.
Interestingly, unlike other Ascians before her, Halamurut encouraged the player to find their own way to deal with the Solstice. The Ascian was only introduced in recent patches, but given how superbly the writers developed its past villains (namely the best Final Fantasy baddie ever, Emet-Selch), I'm eager to see how SE will handle another multidimensional antagonist with a world-ending goal.
Raid content galore
FF14 has always excelled at crossover raid content, whether that be the Yorha: Dark Apocalypse Alliance raid series, developed in collaboration with Nier developers Yoko Taro and Yosuke Saito, or the major raid series inspired by previous Final Fantasy games, like Final Fantasy 3, Final Fantasy 8, Tactics, and more.
Dawntrail's major Alliance raid series, Echoes of Vana'diel, wrapped up with the latest patch, a 24-player crossover celebrating Final Fantasy 6, that offered incredible bosses and a challenging yet rewarding experience.
For Evercold, SE revealed that the Alliance raid series will be based on the hit series Evangelion, titled "Ghosts of Desire", which acclaimed director and animator Mahiro Maeda will join as a special guest artist and designer. Like the Nier raid series, I'm expecting a high-quality experience with some unbelievable boss encounters that push the boundaries of the MMO; however, I'm more excited about the eight-player raid series SE has just announced at FanFest EU.
In the next expansion, FF7 Remake series director Naoki Hamaguchi and Yoshi-P took to the stage to unveil "Beyond the Lifestream," a FF7-themed raid series.
It feels like I've waited years for a proper FF7 collaboration, and the series will come just in time for Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, the final installment in the remake series.
Ahead of Evercold's release, FF14 will also be getting a FF7-themed adjacent feature in the MMO's Gold Saucer on October 28, Keybound Brawler, a new mini-game that will reward players with a glamour bundle inspired by Tifa and Barret's outfits from FF7; a teaser for what's to come.
While SE has yet to share the full raid details, I'm expecting the usual crossover gear (I'm begging for Cloud, Sephiroth, and Aerith outfits, please!), elaborate boss fights inspired by some of FF7's most iconic moments; a confrontation with Safer-Sephiroth while a remixed medley of the FF14 and One-Winged Angel themes plays in the background is surely a given.
Raid maps are also always incredible in FF14; I remember my first time entering the first raid of the YoRHa series and being blown away by the scale of the set pieces and attention to detail, so with Hamaguchi's team working alongside the FF14 team, I'm anticipating something next-level; hopefully a recreation of the dystopian metropolis of Midgar?
It's time for improvements
FF14 has been running for more than a decade after it was rebooted into A Realm Reborn in 2013. Since then, the MMO has seen innumerable changes, including to Jobs, a huge graphics overhaul that modernized the game's visuals, not to mention the upcoming expanded character customization options that players have been yearning for.
But some things have always remained the same, primarily the battle system and activity features. With the release of Evercold, FF14 will receive a significant overhaul with the introduction of the 'Reborn' and 'Evolved' modes.
Reborn mode will be based on the current combat system and Job mechanics, while Evolved mode offers greater emphasis on "job identity", updating combat rotations and changing some abilities, and will only apply to existing Jobs.
It's an exciting new change, because while Jobs occasionally get rebalanced, this is the first time the game is getting a significant gameplay revamp that will allow long-time players to experiment with a new way of playing, and newcomers have two options at their disposal.
What's more, the expansion will also see an overhauled gear progression system with the introduction of 'Adventurer Activity.' In its current state, FF14 requires players to log in every day to complete daily roulettes to earn XP and accrue their weekly cap of 450 Allagan Tomestones, which are exchanged for high-level gear; however, this can be a downside, especially for players who can't log in every day.
With Adventurer Activity, this redesigned framework will change from a daily to a weekly-based reward system, remove the exhausting grind of completing daily roulettes, and instead offer more player freedom.
Adventurer Activity (which may look like a battle pass system, but Yoshi P insisted it absolutely is not!) will let players complete a series of missions to amass activity points instead, whether it be dungeons, PvP, Trials, and more, and SE is even considering allowing unearned points from previous weeks to be collected if players miss out.
This is perfect for people like me who sometimes don't really feel like running roulettes and also gives players a chance to explore other content they wouldn't normally engage with.
Final Fantasy 14: Evercold will arrive in January 2027 for PC, PS4, PS5, Xbox Series X and Series S, and Nintendo Switch 2.

articles.title: TSMC Develops EMIB-like Technology to Compete with Intel
articles.text:
Thursday, July 30th 2026
	
		
	
	
	TSMC Develops EMIB-like Technology to Compete with Intel
TSMC is reportedly developing an advanced packaging technology to rival Intel's Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge (EMIB), which the company internally refers to as EMIB-like. According to sources close to The Information, TSMC's Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate (CoWoS) packaging might lose some customers to Intel's EMIB. As a result, TSMC has begun developing its EMIB-like technology. This development will reportedly be supported by Taiwan's Kinsus Interconnect Technology, which will assist TSMC in developing, scaling, and manufacturing the CoWoS alternative without issues. TSMC currently offers three versions of CoWoS: CoWoS-S, CoWoS-L, and CoWoS-R.
CoWoS-S is the first generation of CoWoS, utilizing a full monolithic silicon interposer with TSVs for maximum routing density and performance. Then, there is CoWoS-L that takes a hybrid approach, replacing the full silicon sheet with a more affordable organic base and embedding small localized silicon bridges (LSI) only where high-speed die-to-die communication occurs. This allows for large layouts to bypass reticle limits through bridge stitching. CoWoS-R is the third option that completely replaces silicon with an organic copper/polymer RDL interposer. It experiences a slight reduction in signal attenuation and routing density, but its mechanical flexibility makes it highly scalable and cost-effective for large-die chips.Intel's advanced packaging portfolio allows designers to use 2D, 2.5D, and 3D building blocks to optimize cost, power, and bandwidth at the system level. EMIB is a substrate-embedded silicon bridge that provides localized, high-density die-to-die routing without the cost and area penalty of a full-size silicon interposer. For example, small silicon EMIB bridges—available in variants like EMIB-M with embedded MIM capacitors and EMIB-T with TSVs—offer low-cost, high-density shoreline connections ideal for logic-to-logic and logic-to-HBM interfaces.
		
		Source:
				The Information			
	
	
	CoWoS-S is the first generation of CoWoS, utilizing a full monolithic silicon interposer with TSVs for maximum routing density and performance. Then, there is CoWoS-L that takes a hybrid approach, replacing the full silicon sheet with a more affordable organic base and embedding small localized silicon bridges (LSI) only where high-speed die-to-die communication occurs. This allows for large layouts to bypass reticle limits through bridge stitching. CoWoS-R is the third option that completely replaces silicon with an organic copper/polymer RDL interposer. It experiences a slight reduction in signal attenuation and routing density, but its mechanical flexibility makes it highly scalable and cost-effective for large-die chips.Intel's advanced packaging portfolio allows designers to use 2D, 2.5D, and 3D building blocks to optimize cost, power, and bandwidth at the system level. EMIB is a substrate-embedded silicon bridge that provides localized, high-density die-to-die routing without the cost and area penalty of a full-size silicon interposer. For example, small silicon EMIB bridges—available in variants like EMIB-M with embedded MIM capacitors and EMIB-T with TSVs—offer low-cost, high-density shoreline connections ideal for logic-to-logic and logic-to-HBM interfaces.

articles.title: Amazon apunta a los cielos: la megaconstelación de más de 5.000 satélites que hablara directo con tu móvil
articles.text:
Amazon apunta a los cielos con un proyecto ambicioso: busca desplegar una megaconstelación de más de 5.000 satélites capaces de comunicarse directamente con teléfonos móviles, sin depender de la infraestructura terrestre tradicional.
Con este movimiento, la compañía pretende llevar servicios de voz, datos y mensajería a zonas donde las redes convencionales no llegan, marcando el inicio de una nueva era en la conectividad global. Aunque la iniciativa aún depende de aprobaciones regulatorias, el plan ya tiene fecha estimada para iniciar el despliegue: 2028.
PUBLICIDAD
Satélites de órbita baja y conexión directa con móviles
Durante décadas, la pérdida de cobertura significaba quedar incomunicado hasta reencontrar señal terrestre. Esto está cambiando gracias a los satélites de órbita baja, que ahora pueden enlazarse directamente con ciertos dispositivos móviles y mantener servicios básicos en lugares remotos o ante fallos en la infraestructura convencional.
La propuesta de Amazon no busca reemplazar las redes tradicionales, sino ampliarlas más allá de sus fronteras actuales. A diferencia de soluciones previas, esta tecnología permitiría a los usuarios mantener conexión en áreas rurales, zonas afectadas por desastres naturales o regiones sin despliegue de antenas terrestres. De este modo, la conectividad deja de depender exclusivamente de la infraestructura instalada en tierra.
PUBLICIDAD
El plan Amazon Leo Direct-to-Device: detalles y objetivos
Amazon ha solicitado autorización a la Comisión Federal de Comunicaciones de Estados Unidos para lanzar hasta 5.105 satélites en órbita baja. Esta futura red, llamada Amazon Leo Direct-to-Device, está pensada para comunicarse con móviles compatibles y dispositivos del Internet de las Cosas, utilizando bandas de espectro que actualmente emplea Globalstar.
El despliegue de esta megaconstelación está previsto para comenzar en 2028, aunque todavía debe pasar por los procesos regulatorios correspondientes. El objetivo no solo abarca la comunicación directa con teléfonos, sino también servicios para vehículos conectados y operaciones remotas fuera del alcance habitual de las redes móviles.
PUBLICIDAD
Cabe señalar que esto permitirá ampliar la cobertura en situaciones y lugares donde los sistemas terrestres no son viables o resultan insuficientes.
Diferencias con la constelación de banda ancha de Amazon
Una pregunta frecuente es si estos nuevos satélites reforzarán la red de banda ancha que Amazon ya está desarrollando. La respuesta es negativa.
El sistema Direct-to-Device funcionará en paralelo a la constelación actual, pero con una misión específica: enlazarse directamente con dispositivos móviles, a diferencia de la red de banda ancha que requiere terminales especializados como Leo Nano, Leo Pro o Leo Ultra.
PUBLICIDAD
Hasta el momento, Amazon ha puesto en órbita más de 390 satélites de su primera red y espera ofrecer servicios fijos a partir de 2026. Sin embargo, la propuesta Direct-to-Device representa un salto cualitativo, ya que busca eliminar la dependencia de hardware especializado y facilitar el acceso directo al usuario final.
Arquitectura de la constelación: cinco capas de cobertura global
El diseño del proyecto contempla la distribución de los satélites en cinco niveles de altitud: 510, 540, 560, 570 y 580 kilómetros sobre la superficie terrestre. Esto permitirá extender la cobertura a latitudes medias, altas y zonas cercanas a los polos, garantizando una conectividad más uniforme.
PUBLICIDAD
Para la comunicación con los dispositivos, se utilizarán las bandas L y S, mientras que los enlaces con estaciones en tierra emplearán las bandas Ka y V. Cada satélite incorporará sistemas avanzados de procesamiento de señales, enlaces ópticos y haces digitales, lo que optimizará el rendimiento y la eficiencia de la red.
La vida útil estimada de estos satélites oscila entre seis y ocho años, tras lo cual serán descendidos a 360 kilómetros para completar su retirada atmosférica de manera controlada.
PUBLICIDAD
Globalstar: la clave estratégica de Amazon
Amazon no partirá desde cero para construir esta nueva red. En abril de 2026 anunció un acuerdo para adquirir Globalstar, operador satelital valorado en unos 11.600 millones de dólares, una transacción que espera concretar en 2027. Esta compra incluye el espectro autorizado, infraestructura ya existente y las constelaciones HIBLEO y C-3.
Estos activos se integrarán con los sistemas de Amazon Leo para operar de manera coordinada y eficiente. Además, Globalstar mantiene acuerdos de largo plazo con empresas como Apple, que utiliza sus satélites para ofrecer servicios de mensajería y asistencia en carretera en ciertos modelos de iPhone y Apple Watch.
PUBLICIDAD
Esta relación anticipa un ecosistema en el que múltiples dispositivos y marcas puedan beneficiarse de la cobertura ampliada que propone Amazon.
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Bon plan – L'ordinateur Portable Samsung Galaxy Book6 Pro 14 (Core Ultra X7) "5 étoiles" à 1 499,99 €
articles.text:
L'ordinateur Portable Samsung Galaxy Book6 Pro 14 (Core Ultra X7) passe sous les 1500 € chez Amazon, Boulanger.com et Rakuten. C'est actuellement l'un des meilleurs produit de notre comparatif.
Le Samsung Galaxy Book6 Pro 14 est un ordinateur portable de la trempe des Asus ZenBook et autres Dell XPS. Son châssis tout en aluminium, sa dalle Oled et son processeur Intel de dernière génération lui permettent de se positionner en alternative crédible (sous Windows) au MacBook Air d’Apple.
Désactivez votre bloqueur de publicités pour accéder à tous les liens ci-dessus.

Performances

Audio

Réparabilité
Points forts
Dalle bien calibrée.
Finition exemplaire.
Polyvalence du processeur.
Autonomie au rendez-vous.
Points faibles
Webcam pas au niveau.
Dotations RAM et SSD faibles.
Logiciels préinstallés.
Le Samsung Galaxy Book6 Pro 14 s'impose comme un ultraportable Windows de premier ordre, porté par une finition en aluminium irréprochable et un superbe écran Oled parfaitement calibré. Grâce à la polyvalence de son processeur Intel Core Ultra X7 et une excellente autonomie en usage courant, il gère sans sourciller la bureautique avancée comme la création de contenu légère. On regrettera simplement une webcam indigne du produit, des logiciels préinstallés superflus et une configuration de base un peu juste en mémoire et en stockage pour une machine de cette trempe.

articles.title: Windows NT 4.0 brought the Win95 UI to servers 30 years ago today — milestone unifying modern Windows OS hit RTM in the Pentium era
articles.text:
Windows NT 4.0 brought the Win95 UI to servers 30 years ago today — milestone unifying modern Windows OS hit RTM in the Pentium era
It was also the last NT release to support Alpha, MIPS, or PowerPC CPU architectures.
Microsoft released Windows NT 4.0 to manufacturing partners on July 31, 1996. Codename Cairo marked an important milestone in the history of Microsoft’s original server OS and would far outlive Microsoft’s original plans as enthusiasts and administrators clung to it, as older readers will be aware. Headlining features of NT 4.0, which made it a winner, include the melding of the intuitive new Windows 95 UI into the fully 32-bit enterprise OS. It was also notable for being the last version of NT to support Alpha, MIPS, or PowerPC CPU architectures.
Historical Windows NT timeline:
- Windows NT Server 3.1 – in 1993, the first version of Windows NT also introduced NTFS
- Windows NT Server 3.5 – in 1994, this update provided integrated support for Winsock and TCP/IP
- Windows NT Server 3.51 - client/server support added in 1995
- Windows NT 4.0 – in 1996, NT got the Windows 95 UI and the familiar My Computer, My Documents, and so on
- Windows 2000 Server – the 5th NT release started a new naming scheme, introduced Active Directory, plus NTFS 3.0 with file system encryption
- Followed by the more modern Server releases…
After the initial Windows NT 4.0 release, Microsoft followed up with a version for embedded systems and its Terminal Server edition.
The Windows NT line was critical to Microsoft as it led the charge against dominant Unix server software ecosystems. Its first public release was in 1993, with version 3.1, but NT 4.0 coupled the underlying data server and personal workstation tooling with Win95 UI elements such as the Start Menu, Taskbar, Task Manager, and so on. It would also support new components like the cryptography API, DCOM, TAPI 2.0, and some DirectX (v2) features.
Despite all the new technology under the hood and the frills of the latest UI, Microsoft’s Windows NT 4.0 launched with remarkably low minimum requirements. Would-be users were recommended to install it on a PC with a CPU that ran at 33 MHz or better, had 32MB of RAM, SVGA graphics, and a hard disk with 256 MB capacity. This was in the Pentium / Pentium Pro era. NT 4.0 would become “the server for the masses,” boasted Microsoft on the OS’s 20th anniversary.
Another reason that NT 4.0 was so important is that it formed the foundation for the Windows XP release (2001), leaving the DOS-based 95, 98/SE, and Me versions of the consumer OS behind as archaic hybrids. In the half-decade between the release of NT 4.0 and XP, Microsoft had a lot of work to do, such as implementing Plug and Play, building out gaming tech, adding WDM drivers, and so on. Thankfully, PCs also grew in muscle, specs, and multimedia capabilities to make the larger and more demanding XP a big hit.
Windows XP landed with a core marketing line that it was “Built on NT technology,” which felt uncomfortable to read if you were from the camp that believed ‘NT’ was short for ‘New Technology.’

It is pretty easy to find an old Cairo release online for retro machine tinkering. Those interested in a more casual poke around in NT 4.0 out of interest, curiosity, or nostalgia will find there are some online installs you can play with via a web browser.
